blocks.text: Memory is one long line of addresses. A grid is two-dimensional. Something has to flatten one into the other, and the choice of *how* is called the **memory layout**.
Take a 2 x 3 grid holding 1 to 6. Memory can only store them in some order. Which order?
There are two sensible answers. Walk along each row in turn, or walk down each column in turn. Both are used in real systems, and they are called **row-major** and **column-major** order.
Whichever is chosen, the point is that the position of a cell can be **computed**, exactly as with a 1D array. For row-major:

blocks.code:
offset of grid[r][c]  =  r x COLUMNS + c
address               =  base + offset x elementSize

blocks.text: Still one multiplication and one addition. Still **O(1)**. Grids are not slower to index than lines — they just need slightly more arithmetic.
Why the layout is worth knowing
If indexing any cell is O(1), why should the layout matter at all? Because of how memory hardware actually behaves.

When the CPU fetches an address, it does not pull back a single byte. It pulls a **cache line** — a contiguous chunk, typically 64 bytes — on the bet that you will want the neighbours soon. That bet is what makes code fast.

items: Walk **along** the memory layout and every fetched chunk contains the next several values you need. Most reads are already in cache.
Walk **across** it and each read lands in a different chunk. Most reads go all the way to main memory.

blocks.text: Both traversals are O(R x C) — big-O cannot tell them apart. On real hardware the difference is often several times over. This is the clearest everyday example of why big-O is necessary but not sufficient, and it is why the next four lessons are worth your attention.
